# Summary

After acute coronary syndrome (ACS), adding a PCSK9 inhibitor to high‑intensity statin therapy produces larger LDL‑C reductions and translates into greater reductions in recurrent cardiovascular events than adding ezetimibe, based on head‑to‑head and class outcomes data. In ODYSSEY OUTCOMES, alirocumab added to maximally tolerated statins reduced LDL‑C by about 50–60 mg/dL at 1–4 months and lowered major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) by 15% over 2.8 years, with independent incremental benefit related to LDL‑C and lipoprotein(a) lowering. In contrast, ezetimibe added to statins yields smaller LDL‑C reductions and has weaker, more modest effects on hard outcomes after ACS; a small randomized trial with atorvastatin±ezetimibe showed improved short‑term composite outcomes with ezetimibe but with a hazard ratio around 2.1 (noting this was a 16‑week trial with specific inclusion criteria and design limitations). PCSK9 inhibitors also show additional benefits on specific outcomes (e.g., limb ischemia/revascularization and VTE‑related events) that are not consistently demonstrated for ezetimibe in ACS.

# LDL‑C Reduction

- Alirocumab: In ODYSSEY OUTCOMES (post‑ACS, on high‑intensity statins), at 4 months alirocumab lowered LDL‑C by approximately 51 mg/dL overall, with similar magnitude in women and men, and reduced MACE (HR 0.85, 95% CI 0.78–0.93) over 2.8 years. The drug also lowered lipoprotein(a) by ~8–10 mg/dL, and reductions in both lipoprotein(a) and corrected LDL‑C independently predicted lower MACE risk after adjustment. <cite id="31948641">Alirocumab reduced corrected LDL‑C by 51.1 mg/dL and lowered MACE (HR 0.85, 95% CI 0.78–0.93); reductions in lipoprotein(a) and corrected LDL‑C independently predicted lower MACE risk after adjustment</cite> <cite id="38960812">At 4 months, alirocumab lowered LDL‑C by 49.4 mg/dL in women and 54.0 mg/dL in men and reduced MACE, death, and total cardiovascular events similarly in both sexes</cite> <cite id="32223446">With alirocumab, median relative reductions were 23.5% in lipoprotein(a) and 70.6% in LDL‑C (corrected)</cite>.

- Ezetimibe: In a 16‑week randomized trial in recent ACS, adding ezetimibe to atorvastatin reduced the composite of death/MI/unstable angina/revascularization/stroke (Kaplan–Meier at 16 weeks: 88.1% vs 77.0%; ARR 11.1 percentage points; HR 2.099, 95% CI 1.165–3.781), but this was a short‑term study and the effect size reflects a relatively modest LDL‑C reduction compared with PCSK9 inhibitors. <cite id="28553847">In a 16‑week randomized trial in ACS, atorvastatin±ezetimibe improved event‑free survival (88.1% vs 77.0% at 16 weeks; HR 2.099, 95% CI 1.165–3.781), with similar effects in men and women</cite>.

# Cardiovascular Outcomes

- Alirocumab (PCSK9 inhibitor): In ODYSSEY OUTCOMES, the absolute risk reduction in MACE was ~15% over 2.8 years, with stronger benefit in patients with higher baseline LDL‑C and in analyses emphasizing very low achieved LDL‑C levels (<0.39 mmol/L) followed by statin continuation, where a short "legacy" benefit persisted. <cite id="36879424">A short period of LDL‑C <0.39 mmol/L achieved with statin plus alirocumab, followed by statin monotherapy, was associated with lower MACE (HR 0.72, 95% CI 0.51–0.997) than statin monotherapy; clinical benefit persisted for several years</cite> <cite id="31948641">Alirocumab reduced MACE (HR 0.85, 95% CI 0.78–0.93), with independent predictive value of LDL‑C and lipoprotein(a) reductions</cite>. # Comparative Interpretation

- Magnitude of LDL‑C lowering: Alirocumab produces roughly 50–60 mg/dL LDL‑C reduction at 4 months on a high‑intensity statin, whereas ezetimibe provides a smaller incremental effect; this magnitude difference aligns with the larger observed event reductions with PCSK9 inhibitors in post‑ACS populations. <cite id="31948641">Alirocumab lowered corrected LDL‑C by ~51 mg/dL at 4 months</cite> <cite id="38960812">At 4 months, LDL‑C reductions were ~49–54 mg/dL by sex</cite> <cite id="28553847">Ezetimibe addition improved short‑term composite outcomes but reflects a smaller LDL‑C effect compared with PCSK9 inhibitors</cite>.

- Timing and sequencing: Current expert guidance supports initiating high‑intensity statins immediately after ACS and using PCSK9 inhibitors after a 2–3 month run‑in on maximally tolerated statins; early PCSK9 use in the acute phase may be justified in selected high‑risk patients but requires further study. - LDL‑C: PCSK9 inhibitors lower LDL‑C substantially more than ezetimibe when added to high‑intensity statins after ACS. <cite id="31948641">Alirocumab reduced LDL‑C by ~51 mg/dL at 4 months</cite> <cite id="38960812">LDL‑C reductions were ~49–54 mg/dL by sex</cite> <cite id="28553847">Ezetimibe produced smaller incremental LDL‑C and short‑term composite outcome benefits</cite>.

- Events: Adding a PCSK9 inhibitor to high‑intensity statins reduces recurrent cardiovascular events more than adding ezetimibe, with clear benefits observed in MACE and organ‑specific outcomes, while ezetimibe's incremental benefit after ACS is smaller and most evident over short horizons. <cite id="31948641">Alirocumab reduced MACE (HR 0.85)</cite> <cite id="36879424">Very low LDL‑C periods with alirocumab were associated with lower MACE and persistent legacy benefit</cite> <cite id="32223446">PCSK9 inhibition reduced PAD events and showed a trend for VTE reduction</cite> <cite id="28553847">Ezetimibe improved 16‑week composite outcomes vs statin monotherapy (HR 2.099)</cite>.

- Safety: Both classes are generally well tolerated in the post‑ACS setting; neurocognitive concerns are not specifically linked to PCSK9 inhibitors in post‑ACS trials, and ezetimibe has a favorable safety profile. <cite id="30015301">Very low LDL‑C below 1 mmol/L has not shown reported safety issues, particularly neurocognitive, with PCSK9 mAbs</cite>.

data.title: Effect of Alirocumab on Lipoprotein(a) and Cardiovascular Risk After Acute Coronary Syndrome.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
Lipoprotein(a) concentration is associated with cardiovascular events. Alirocumab, a proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 inhibitor, lowers lipoprotein(a) and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C).
OBJECTIVES
A pre-specified analysis of the placebo-controlled ODYSSEY Outcomes trial in patients with recent acute coronary syndrome (ACS) determined whether alirocumab-induced changes in lipoprotein(a) and LDL-C independently predicted major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE).
METHODS
One to 12 months after ACS, 18,924 patients on high-intensity statin therapy were randomized to alirocumab or placebo and followed for 2.8 years (median). Lipoprotein(a) was measured at randomization and 4 and 12 months thereafter. The primary MACE outcome was coronary heart disease death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, ischemic stroke, or hospitalization for unstable angina.
RESULTS
Baseline lipoprotein(a) levels (median: 21.2 mg/dl; interquartile range [IQR]: 6.7 to 59.6 mg/dl) and LDL-C [corrected for cholesterol content in lipoprotein(a)] predicted MACE. Alirocumab reduced lipoprotein(a) by 5.0 mg/dl (IQR: 0 to 13.5 mg/dl), corrected LDL-C by 51.1 mg/dl (IQR: 33.7 to 67.2 mg/dl), and reduced the risk of MACE (hazard ratio [HR]: 0.85; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.78 to 0.93). Alirocumab-induced reductions of lipoprotein(a) and corrected LDL-C independently predicted lower risk of MACE, after adjustment for baseline concentrations of both lipoproteins and demographic and clinical characteristics. A 1-mg/dl reduction in lipoprotein(a) with alirocumab was associated with a HR of 0.994 (95% CI: 0.990 to 0.999; p = 0.0081).
CONCLUSIONS
Baseline lipoprotein(a) and corrected LDL-C levels and their reductions by alirocumab predicted the risk of MACE after recent ACS. Lipoprotein(a) lowering by alirocumab is an independent contributor to MACE reduction, which suggests that lipoprotein(a) should be an independent treatment target after ACS. (ODYSSEY Outcomes: Evaluation of Cardiovascular Outcomes After an Acute Coronary Syndrome During Treatment With Alirocumab; NCT01663402).

data.title: Transiently achieved very low LDL-cholesterol levels by statin and alirocumab after acute coronary syndrome are associated with cardiovascular risk reduction: the ODYSSEY OUTCOMES trial.
data.abstract:
AIMS
Long-term, placebo-controlled cholesterol-lowering trials have demonstrated legacy effects (clinical benefits that persist or emerge after trial end). It is unknown whether legacy effects follow a short period of very low low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) levels achieved with statin plus PCSK9 inhibitor.
METHODS AND RESULTS
In 18,924 patients post-acute coronary syndrome, the ODYSSEY OUTCOMES trial compared the PCSK9 inhibitor alirocumab with placebo, each added to high-intensity or maximum-tolerated statin therapy. Patients with two consecutive LDL-C levels <0.39 mmol/L (15 mg/dL) on alirocumab had blinded placebo substitution for the remainder of the trial with continued statin treatment. In post hoc analyses, major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) in these patients were compared to MACE in propensity score-matched patients from the placebo group with similar baseline characteristics and study medication adherence. In the alirocumab group, 730 patients had blinded placebo substitution at a median 8.3 months from randomization, after a median 6.0 months with LDL-C < 0.39 mmol/L. They were matched to 1460 placebo patients. Both groups had lower baseline LDL-C and lipoprotein(a) and better study medication adherence than the overall cohort. Over a median follow-up of 2.8 years, MACE occurred in 47 (6.4%) alirocumab patients with limited-duration, very low achieved LDL-C versus 122 (8.4%) matched placebo patients (treatment hazard ratio 0.72; 95% confidence interval 0.51, 0.997; P = 0.047).
CONCLUSIONS
A short period of LDL-C levels <0.39 mmol/L achieved with statin and alirocumab, followed by statin monotherapy, was associated with lower risk of MACE than statin monotherapy throughout the observation period. Clinical benefit persisted for several years.
TRIAL REGISTRATION
ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01663402.

data.title: Alirocumab and cardiovascular outcomes according to sex and lipoprotein(a) after acute coronary syndrome: a report from the ODYSSEY OUTCOMES study.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
The ODYSSEY OUTCOMES trial (NCT01663402) compared the effects of the proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 inhibitor alirocumab with placebo on major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) in patients with recent acute coronary syndrome (ACS).
OBJECTIVE
We assessed efficacy and safety of alirocumab versus placebo according to sex and lipoprotein(a) level.
METHODS
This prespecified analysis compared the effects of alirocumab versus placebo on lipoproteins, MACE (coronary heart disease death, non-fatal myocardial infarction, fatal/non-fatal ischemic stroke, unstable angina requiring hospitalization), death, total cardiovascular events, and adverse events in 4762 women and 14,162 men followed for a median of 2.8 years. In post-hoc analysis, we evaluated total cardiovascular events according to sex, baseline lipoprotein(a), and treatment.
RESULTS
Women were older, had higher baseline low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) levels (89.6 vs 85.3 mg/dL) and lipoprotein(a) (28.0 vs 19.3 mg/dL) and had more co-morbidities than men. At 4 months, alirocumab lowered LDL-C by 49.4 mg/dL in women and 54.0 mg/dL in men and lipoprotein(a) by 9.7 and 8.1 mg/dL, respectively (both p < 0.0001). Alirocumab reduced MACE, death, and total cardiovascular events similarly in both sexes. In the placebo group, lipoprotein(a) was a risk factor for total cardiovascular events in women and men. In both sexes, reduction of total cardiovascular events was greater at higher baseline lipoprotein(a), but this effect was more evident in women than men (p interaction =0.08). Medication adherence and adverse event rates were similar in both sexes.
CONCLUSIONS
Alirocumab improves cardiovascular outcomes after ACS irrespective of sex. Reduction of total cardiovascular events was greater at higher baseline lipoprotein(a).

data.title: Peripheral Artery Disease and Venous Thromboembolic Events After Acute Coronary Syndrome: Role of Lipoprotein(a) and Modification by Alirocumab: Prespecified Analysis of the ODYSSEY OUTCOMES Randomized Clinical Trial.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
Patients with acute coronary syndrome are at risk for peripheral artery disease (PAD) events and venous thromboembolism (VTE). PCSK9 (proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9) inhibitors reduce lipoprotein(a) and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) levels. Our objective was to ascertain whether PCSK9 inhibition reduces the risk of PAD events or VTE after acute coronary syndrome, and if such effects are related to levels of lipoprotein(a) or LDL-C.
METHODS
This was a prespecified analysis of the ODYSSEY OUTCOMES randomized clinical trial (Evaluation of Cardiovascular Outcomes After an Acute Coronary Syndrome), which was conducted in 18 924 patients with recent acute coronary syndrome on intensive or maximum-tolerated statin treatment who were randomized to the PCSK9 inhibitor alirocumab or placebo. In a prespecified analysis, PAD events (critical limb ischemia, limb revascularization, or amputation for ischemia) and VTE (deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism) were assessed. LDL-C was corrected (LDL-C corrected ) for cholesterol content in lipoprotein(a).
RESULTS
At baseline, median lipoprotein(a) and LDL-C corrected were 21 and 75 mg/dL, respectively; with alirocumab, median relative reductions were 23.5% and 70.6%, respectively. PAD events and VTE occurred in 246 and 92 patients, respectively. In the placebo group, risk of PAD events was related to baseline quartile of lipoprotein(a) ( P trend =0.0021), and tended to associate with baseline quartile of LDL-C corrected ( P trend =0.06); VTE tended to associate with baseline quartile of lipoprotein(a) ( P trend =0.06), but not LDL-C corrected ( P trend =0.85). Alirocumab reduced risk of PAD events (hazard ratio [HR], 0.69 [95% CI, 0.54-0.89]; P =0.004), with nonsignificantly fewer VTE events (HR, 0.67 [95% CI, 0.44-1.01]; P =0.06). Reduction in PAD events with alirocumab was associated with baseline quartile of lipoprotein(a) ( P trend =0.03), but not LDL-C corrected ( P trend =0.50). With alirocumab, the change from baseline to Month 4 in lipoprotein(a), but not LDL-C corrected , was associated with the risk of VTE and the composite of VTE and PAD events.
CONCLUSIONS
In statin-treated patients with recent acute coronary syndrome, risk of PAD events is related to lipoprotein(a) level and is reduced by alirocumab, particularly among those with high lipoprotein(a). Further study is required to confirm whether risk of VTE is related to lipoprotein(a) level and its reduction with alirocumab. data.title: PCSK9 inhibitors and cardiovascular outcomes.
data.abstract: Introduction : Dyslipidemia, particularly elevated low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C), is a key risk factor for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD), and lipid-lowering drugs are beneficial for the primary and secondary prevention of cardiovascular (CV) disease. While statins are clear first-line drugs, new drug developments such as proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (PCSK9) inhibitors have been shown to improve cardiovascular outcomes when added to statins. Evolocumab reduced the risk of cardiovascular events in patients with ASCVD when added to maximally tolerated statin therapy (± ezetimibe), and recent data from the ODYSSEY OUTCOMES trial indicate that alirocumab added to maximally tolerated statin therapy (± other lipid-lowering drugs) reduces the risk of cardiovascular events in patients with a recent acute coronary syndrome. In this article the authors review the available data on the effect of PCSK9 inhibitors on cardiovascular outcomes. Areas covered : This article reviews the available data on the effect of PCSK9 inhibitors on CV outcomes. Relevant papers were identified from a search of PubMed/Medline and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL). Expert opinion : The authors conclude that PCSK9 inhibitors provide substantial and durable reductions in LDL-C levels and improve cardiovascular outcomes.

data.title: Interpreting the Findings From the Recent PCSK9 Monoclonal Antibody Cardiovascular Outcomes Trials.
data.abstract: The recent development of monoclonal antibodies targeted to proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (PCSK9), e.g., PCSK9 inhibitors has revolutionized the landscape of lipid management. Many clinical trials assessing this class have demonstrated remarkable and consistent reductions in low-density lipoprotein-cholesterol. Moreover, the GLAGOV trial demonstrated the efficacy of evolocumab, when added to statin therapy, in reducing the progression of atherosclerosis measured by serial intravascular ultrasound, with the first suggestion of continued benefit down to LDL-C levels of 0.5 mmol/L (20 mg/dL). This trial was followed by the FOURIER Cardiovascular Outcomes trial in more than 27,000 patients with stable atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) where evolocumab reduced the primary endpoint of atherosclerotic events by 15%, without significant safety differences between treatment groups. Furthermore, subgroup analyses suggested greater benefits seen in those with longer exposure to evolocumab recent acute coronary syndrome, multiple myocardial infarctions, multivessel coronary artery disease, peripheral arterial disease, as well as the subgroup who achieved very low low-density lipoprotein-cholesterol levels of below 0.3 mmol/L (10 mg/dL). Moreover, the EBBINGHAUS substudy demonstrated no differences in objectively measured cognitive function between treatment groups. The SPIRE 2 trial evaluating bococizumab in high-risk patients with baseline LDL-C ≥2.6 mmol/L (100 mg/dL) demonstrated significant atherosclerotic risk reduction, but the trial and further development of the drug was prematurely discontinued due to substantial attenuation of the LDL-C effect over time due to the development of neutralizing antibodies. Finally, the ODYSSEY Cardiovascular Outcomes trial testing alirocumab in subjects with recent (<1 year) acute coronary syndrome demonstrated a 15% relative risk reduction in the primary composite outcome, as well as a significant reduction in total mortality. Greater benefits were noted in those whose LDL-C at baseline was 2.6 mmol/L (100 mg/dL) or greater. These trials collectively demonstrate the added efficacy of PCSK9 inhibitors over moderate and high-intensity statin therapy for unprecedented low-density lipoprotein-cholesterol reduction and incremental ASCVD risk reduction.

data.title: Lipid management in ACS: Should we go lower faster?
data.abstract: Low-density lipoprotein-cholesterol (LDL-C) is a well-accepted causal risk factor for athero-thrombotic cardiovascular disease, as demonstrated in large epidemiological studies, including Mendelian randomization data. Several randomized controlled trials and meta-analyzes have shown that lipid lowering therapies, such as statins and more recently the non-statin agents ezetimibe and Proprotein Convertase Subtilisin Kexin type 9 (PCSK9) monoclonal antibodies (mAb), reduce cardiovascular events across a broad range of baseline LDL-C levels. Over time, the recommended target for LDL-C has become more stringent, moving from 2.6 mmol/l to 1.8 mmol/l in very high-risk patients. It is currently recommended to start high intensity statin treatment immediately after acute coronary syndromes (ACS) to maximally and rapidly reduce LDL-C. The novel treatment options enable the achievement of very low LDL-C levels below 1 mmol/l, with no reported safety issues, in particular with regard to neurocognitive events. However, current evidence supports the use of PCSK9 mAb treatment in ACS patients only after an initial 2-3 month run-up treatment adaptation period with maximally tolerated statin. The use of PCSK9 mAb immediately in the acute phase of ACS (<1 month) remains to be studied. Some data suggest that circulating PCSK9 increases coronary plaque vulnerability, inflammation as well as platelet aggregation in the acute phase of ACS, potentially justifying earlier PSCK9 mAb treatment initiation. As the use of novel treatment combinations in ACS is further explored to widen the perspectives of a more personalized approach for the management of ACS based on individual patient risk profile and baseline LDL-C values, their relative cost-effectiveness will also need to be assessed.

data.title: The short-term effect of atorvastatin plus ezetimibe therapy versus atorvastatin monotherapy on clinical outcome in acute coronary syndrome patients by gender.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
Atorvastatin reduces low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) levels and the risk of cardiovascular events, but whether the addition of ezetimibe (EZE), a non-statin drug that reduces intestinal cholesterol absorption, can reduce the rate of cardiovascular events further, and if there any sex differences, is not known.
AIM
To evaluate the effects of atorvastatin and EZE combination in acute coronary syndrome (ACS) patients on the incidence of composite endpoint in short-term follow-up and to assess differences according their gender.
METHODS
We conducted a 16-week, single-centre, prospective, randomised, open-label clinical trial involving 323 patients who had been hospitalised for an ACS within the preceding 14 days. They received atorvastatin 20 mg for 28 days, and after that 292 patients who had LDL-C levels ≥ 1.81 mmol/L were randomised to EZE 10 mg/day co-administered with atorvastatin therapy (EZE + statin) or double their current atorvastatin dose. The primary endpoint was a composite of cardiovascular death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, unstable angina requiring rehospitalisation, coronary revascularisation (≥ 30 days after randomisation), or nonfatal stroke.
RESULTS
The Kaplan-Meier event-free survival rate at 16 weeks was 88.1% in the EZE + statin group patients and 77.0% in the atorvastatin monotherapy group (absolute risk reduction: 11.1 percentage points; hazard ratio: 2.099; 95% confidence interval: 1.165-3.781; p = 0.014). The log rank test indicated that there was not a statistically significant difference between male and female survival rates in both treatment groups (p = 0.897).
CONCLUSIONS
The results of our study demonstrated that when added to statin therapy, EZE resulted in improved cardiovascular outcomes, and the response to atorvastatin and EZE combination was similar for both men and women.

data.abstract: In 2016, the American College of Cardiology published the first expert consensus decision pathway (ECDP) on the role of non-statin therapies for low-density lipoprotein (LDL)-cholesterol lowering in the management of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) risk. Since the publication of that document, additional evidence and perspectives have emerged from randomized clinical trials and other sources, particularly considering the longer-term efficacy and safety of proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin 9 (PCSK9) inhibitors in secondary prevention of ASCVD. Most notably, the FOURIER (Further Cardiovascular Outcomes Research with PCSK9 Inhibition in Subjects with Elevated Risk) trial and SPIRE-1 and -2 (Studies of PCSK9 Inhibition and the Reduction of Vascular Events), assessing evolocumab and bococizumab, respectively, have published final results of cardiovascular outcomes trials in patients with clinical ASCVD and in a smaller number of high-risk primary prevention patients. In addition, further evidence on the types of patients most likely to benefit from the use of ezetimibe in addition to statin therapy after acute coronary syndrome has been published. Based on results from these important analyses, the ECDP writing committee judged that it would be desirable to provide a focused update to help guide clinicians more clearly on decision making regarding the use of ezetimibe and PCSK9 inhibitors in patients with clinical ASCVD with or without comorbidities. In the following summary table, changes from the 2016 ECDP to the 2017 ECDP Focused Update are highlighted, and a brief rationale is provided. The content of the full document has been changed accordingly, with more extensive and detailed guidance regarding decision making provided both in the text and in the updated algorithms. Revised recommendations are provided for patients with clinical ASCVD with or without comorbidities on statin therapy for secondary prevention. The ECDP writing committee judged that these new data did not warrant changes to the decision pathways and algorithms regarding the use of ezetimibe or PCSK9 inhibitors in primary prevention patients with LDL-C <190 mg/dL with or without diabetes mellitus or patients without ASCVD and LDL-C ≥190 mg/dL not due to secondary causes. Based on feedback and further deliberation, the ECDP writing committee down-graded recommendations regarding bile acid sequestrant use, recommending bile acid sequestrants only as optional secondary agents for consideration in patients intolerant to ezetimibe. For clarification, the writing committee has also included new information on diagnostic categories of heterozygous and homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia, based on clinical criteria with and without genetic testing. Other changes to the original document were kept to a minimum to provide consistent guidance to clinicians, unless there was a compelling reason or new evidence, in which case justification is provided.

data.title: Lipid management in ACS: Should we go lower faster?
data.abstract: Low-density lipoprotein-cholesterol (LDL-C) is a well-accepted causal risk factor for athero-thrombotic cardiovascular disease, as demonstrated in large epidemiological studies, including Mendelian randomization data. Several randomized controlled trials and meta-analyzes have shown that lipid lowering therapies, such as statins and more recently the non-statin agents ezetimibe and Proprotein Convertase Subtilisin Kexin type 9 (PCSK9) monoclonal antibodies (mAb), reduce cardiovascular events across a broad range of baseline LDL-C levels. Over time, the recommended target for LDL-C has become more stringent, moving from 2.6 mmol/l to 1.8 mmol/l in very high-risk patients. It is currently recommended to start high intensity statin treatment immediately after acute coronary syndromes (ACS) to maximally and rapidly reduce LDL-C. The novel treatment options enable the achievement of very low LDL-C levels below 1 mmol/l, with no reported safety issues, in particular with regard to neurocognitive events. However, current evidence supports the use of PCSK9 mAb treatment in ACS patients only after an initial 2-3 month run-up treatment adaptation period with maximally tolerated statin. The use of PCSK9 mAb immediately in the acute phase of ACS (<1 month) remains to be studied. Some data suggest that circulating PCSK9 increases coronary plaque vulnerability, inflammation as well as platelet aggregation in the acute phase of ACS, potentially justifying earlier PSCK9 mAb treatment initiation. As the use of novel treatment combinations in ACS is further explored to widen the perspectives of a more personalized approach for the management of ACS based on individual patient risk profile and baseline LDL-C values, their relative cost-effectiveness will also need to be assessed.

data.title: The short-term effect of atorvastatin plus ezetimibe therapy versus atorvastatin monotherapy on clinical outcome in acute coronary syndrome patients by gender.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
Atorvastatin reduces low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) levels and the risk of cardiovascular events, but whether the addition of ezetimibe (EZE), a non-statin drug that reduces intestinal cholesterol absorption, can reduce the rate of cardiovascular events further, and if there any sex differences, is not known.
AIM
To evaluate the effects of atorvastatin and EZE combination in acute coronary syndrome (ACS) patients on the incidence of composite endpoint in short-term follow-up and to assess differences according their gender.
METHODS
We conducted a 16-week, single-centre, prospective, randomised, open-label clinical trial involving 323 patients who had been hospitalised for an ACS within the preceding 14 days. They received atorvastatin 20 mg for 28 days, and after that 292 patients who had LDL-C levels ≥ 1.81 mmol/L were randomised to EZE 10 mg/day co-administered with atorvastatin therapy (EZE + statin) or double their current atorvastatin dose. The primary endpoint was a composite of cardiovascular death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, unstable angina requiring rehospitalisation, coronary revascularisation (≥ 30 days after randomisation), or nonfatal stroke.
RESULTS
The Kaplan-Meier event-free survival rate at 16 weeks was 88.1% in the EZE + statin group patients and 77.0% in the atorvastatin monotherapy group (absolute risk reduction: 11.1 percentage points; hazard ratio: 2.099; 95% confidence interval: 1.165-3.781; p = 0.014). The log rank test indicated that there was not a statistically significant difference between male and female survival rates in both treatment groups (p = 0.897).
CONCLUSIONS
The results of our study demonstrated that when added to statin therapy, EZE resulted in improved cardiovascular outcomes, and the response to atorvastatin and EZE combination was similar for both men and women.

# Summary

After acute coronary syndrome (ACS), adding a PCSK9 inhibitor to high‑intensity statin therapy produces larger LDL‑C reductions and translates into greater reductions in recurrent cardiovascular events than adding ezetimibe, based on head‑to‑head and class outcomes data. In ODYSSEY OUTCOMES, alirocumab added to maximally tolerated statins reduced LDL‑C by about 50–60 mg/dL at 1–4 months and lowered major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) by 15% over 2.8 years, with independent incremental benefit related to LDL‑C and lipoprotein(a) lowering. In contrast, ezetimibe added to statins yields smaller LDL‑C reductions and has weaker, more modest effects on hard outcomes after ACS; a small randomized trial with atorvastatin±ezetimibe showed improved short‑term composite outcomes with ezetimibe but with a hazard ratio around 2.1 (noting this was a 16‑week trial with specific inclusion criteria and design limitations). PCSK9 inhibitors also show additional benefits on specific outcomes (e.g., limb ischemia/revascularization and VTE‑related events) that are not consistently demonstrated for ezetimibe in ACS.

# LDL‑C Reduction

- Alirocumab: In ODYSSEY OUTCOMES (post‑ACS, on high‑intensity statins), at 4 months alirocumab lowered LDL‑C by approximately 51 mg/dL overall, with similar magnitude in women and men, and reduced MACE (HR 0.85, 95% CI 0.78–0.93) over 2.8 years. The drug also lowered lipoprotein(a) by ~8–10 mg/dL, and reductions in both lipoprotein(a) and corrected LDL‑C independently predicted lower MACE risk after adjustment. <cite id="31948641">Alirocumab reduced corrected LDL‑C by 51.1 mg/dL and lowered MACE (HR 0.85, 95% CI 0.78–0.93); reductions in lipoprotein(a) and corrected LDL‑C independently predicted lower MACE risk after adjustment</cite> <cite id="38960812">At 4 months, alirocumab lowered LDL‑C by 49.4 mg/dL in women and 54.0 mg/dL in men and reduced MACE, death, and total cardiovascular events similarly in both sexes</cite> <cite id="32223446">With alirocumab, median relative reductions were 23.5% in lipoprotein(a) and 70.6% in LDL‑C (corrected)</cite>.

- Ezetimibe: In a 16‑week randomized trial in recent ACS, adding ezetimibe to atorvastatin reduced the composite of death/MI/unstable angina/revascularization/stroke (Kaplan–Meier at 16 weeks: 88.1% vs 77.0%; ARR 11.1 percentage points; HR 2.099, 95% CI 1.165–3.781), but this was a short‑term study and the effect size reflects a relatively modest LDL‑C reduction compared with PCSK9 inhibitors. <cite id="28553847">In a 16‑week randomized trial in ACS, atorvastatin±ezetimibe improved event‑free survival (88.1% vs 77.0% at 16 weeks; HR 2.099, 95% CI 1.165–3.781), with similar effects in men and women</cite>.

# Cardiovascular Outcomes

- Alirocumab (PCSK9 inhibitor): In ODYSSEY OUTCOMES, the absolute risk reduction in MACE was ~15% over 2.8 years, with stronger benefit in patients with higher baseline LDL‑C and in analyses emphasizing very low achieved LDL‑C levels (<0.39 mmol/L) followed by statin continuation, where a short "legacy" benefit persisted. <cite id="36879424">A short period of LDL‑C <0.39 mmol/L achieved with statin plus alirocumab, followed by statin monotherapy, was associated with lower MACE (HR 0.72, 95% CI 0.51–0.997) than statin monotherapy; clinical benefit persisted for several years</cite> <cite id="31948641">Alirocumab reduced MACE (HR 0.85, 95% CI 0.78–0.93), with independent predictive value of LDL‑C and lipoprotein(a) reductions</cite>. PCSK9 inhibition also reduced PAD events (HR ~0.69) and showed a trend toward fewer VTE events, with benefit particularly in patients with high lipoprotein(a). <cite id="32223446">Alirocumab reduced PAD events (HR 0.69 [95% CI 0.54–0.89]) and nonsignificantly reduced VTE; PAD benefit was related to baseline lipoprotein(a) quartile</cite>.

- Ezetimibe: Expert pathway updates and trial syntheses indicate that ezetimibe added to statins reduces LDL‑C modestly and yields smaller absolute risk reductions in hard cardiovascular outcomes after ACS compared with PCSK9 inhibitors. The 2017 ACC expert consensus update highlights that while ezetimibe can be beneficial, PCSK9 inhibitors demonstrate more substantial and consistent risk reduction in secondary prevention settings. <cite id="28886926">The 2017 ACC focused update notes additional evidence on patients most likely to benefit from ezetimibe after ACS, but overall supports stronger risk reduction with PCSK9 inhibitors in secondary prevention</cite> <cite id="30015301">Expert review emphasizes that PCSK9 mAbs achieve much greater LDL‑C lowering and incremental ASCVD risk reduction compared with ezetimibe, with immediate post‑ACS use of PCSK9 inhibitors favored after a statin run‑in</cite>.

# Comparative Interpretation

- Magnitude of LDL‑C lowering: Alirocumab produces roughly 50–60 mg/dL LDL‑C reduction at 4 months on a high‑intensity statin, whereas ezetimibe provides a smaller incremental effect; this magnitude difference aligns with the larger observed event reductions with PCSK9 inhibitors in post‑ACS populations. <cite id="31948641">Alirocumab lowered corrected LDL‑C by ~51 mg/dL at 4 months</cite> <cite id="38960812">At 4 months, LDL‑C reductions were ~49–54 mg/dL by sex</cite> <cite id="28553847">Ezetimibe addition improved short‑term composite outcomes but reflects a smaller LDL‑C effect compared with PCSK9 inhibitors</cite>.

- Hard outcomes: In a large, placebo‑controlled post‑ACS cohort, PCSK9 inhibition reduced MACE by ~15% and showed benefits in organ‑specific events (PAD, VTE), while the randomized ezetimibe trial demonstrated improved short‑term composite events but with a relatively higher hazard ratio, underscoring the relative strength of PCSK9 inhibitors for risk reduction. <cite id="31948641">Alirocumab reduced MACE (HR 0.85)</cite> <cite id="36879424">Very low LDL‑C periods with alirocumab were associated with lower MACE and persistent legacy benefit</cite> <cite id="32223446">PCSK9 inhibition reduced PAD events and showed a trend for VTE reduction</cite> <cite id="28553847">Ezetimibe improved 16‑week composite outcomes vs statin monotherapy (HR ~2.1)</cite>.

# Practical Considerations

- Timing and sequencing: Current expert guidance supports initiating high‑intensity statins immediately after ACS and using PCSK9 inhibitors after a 2–3 month run‑in on maximally tolerated statins; early PCSK9 use in the acute phase may be justified in selected high‑risk patients but requires further study. Ezetimibe can be added to a stable high‑intensity statin regimen when further LDL‑C lowering is desired, with expected modest incremental benefit on outcomes. <cite id="30015301">Guidance recommends high‑intensity statins immediately after ACS and PCSK9 mAbs after 2–3 months on maximally tolerated statins; early PCSK9 use in ACS <1 month remains to be studied</cite> <cite id="28886926">The ACC focused update integrates evidence on ezetimibe use after ACS and maintains that PCSK9 inhibitors provide greater incremental benefit in secondary prevention</cite>.

# Bottom Line

- LDL‑C: PCSK9 inhibitors lower LDL‑C substantially more than ezetimibe when added to high‑intensity statins after ACS. <cite id="31948641">Alirocumab reduced LDL‑C by ~51 mg/dL at 4 months</cite> <cite id="38960812">LDL‑C reductions were ~49–54 mg/dL by sex</cite> <cite id="28553847">Ezetimibe produced smaller incremental LDL‑C and short‑term composite outcome benefits</cite>.

- Events: Adding a PCSK9 inhibitor to high‑intensity statins reduces recurrent cardiovascular events more than adding ezetimibe, with clear benefits observed in MACE and organ‑specific outcomes, while ezetimibe's incremental benefit after ACS is smaller and most evident over short horizons. <cite id="31948641">Alirocumab reduced MACE (HR 0.85)</cite> <cite id="36879424">Very low LDL‑C periods with alirocumab were associated with lower MACE and persistent legacy benefit</cite> <cite id="32223446">PCSK9 inhibition reduced PAD events and showed a trend for VTE reduction</cite> <cite id="28553847">Ezetimibe improved 16‑week composite outcomes vs statin monotherapy (HR 2.099)</cite>.

- Safety: Both classes are generally well tolerated in the post‑ACS setting; neurocognitive concerns are not specifically linked to PCSK9 inhibitors in post‑ACS trials, and ezetimibe has a favorable safety profile. <cite id="30015301">Very low LDL‑C below 1 mmol/L has not shown reported safety issues, particularly neurocognitive, with PCSK9 mAbs</cite>.

Overall, for very high‑risk post‑ACS patients not achieving target LDL‑C on high‑intensity statins, a PCSK9 inhibitor is the preferred non‑statin add‑on to maximize LDL‑C lowering and reduce recurrent events, whereas ezetimibe offers a smaller, incremental benefit and is reasonable when maximal tolerated statin therapy has been established and LDL‑C remains only modestly elevated. <cite id="30015301">PCSK9 mAbs enable achievement of very low LDL‑C with no reported safety issues and provide incremental ASCVD risk reduction</cite> <cite id="28886926">Expert consensus supports stronger risk reduction with PCSK9 inhibitors than ezetimibe in secondary prevention after ACS</cite>.

<snippet id="34693803">Title: Systemic lupus erythematosus and pregnancy: A retrospective single-center study of 215 pregnancies from Portugal.
Authors: Braga, António, Barros, Tânia, Faria, Raquel et al. | Year: 2021 | Journal: Lupus
Abstract: OBJECTIVE
Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a life-threatening disorder that affects women at reproductive age. We evaluate the clinical impact of pregnancy in a cohort of Portuguese SLE patients and the risk factors associated with maternal and fetal adverse outcomes.
METHODS
A retrospective observational study that included all pregnant women with SLE managed at a Portuguese tertiary hospital, between January 1993 and December 2019. Baseline maternal information was collected, and maternal-fetal and neonatal outcomes were evaluated. Disease activity before and during pregnancy was assessed.
RESULTS
We included 215 pregnancies from 143 patients. Lupus nephritis was present in 20.0% and antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) in 21.9% of the cases. Preconception consultation was performed in 86.9% of the pregnancies, and 92.5% of the patients had no or low disease activity at conception. During gestation, 79.6% of the patients were under treatment, and hydroxychloroquine (HCQ) was the most commonly used drug (63.7%). Low-dose acetylsalicylic acid (ASA) was prescribed at conception in 87.9% of the patients. The live birth rate was 84.2%. An adverse pregnancy outcome (APO) occurred in 41.4% of the pregnancies. A miscarriage rate of 15.3% and a preterm delivery rate of 15.4% were found. Preeclampsia and fetal growth restriction complicated 13.1% and 14.0% of the gestations, respectively. Neonatal lupus occurred in 7.1% of the newborns, and there were 2 cases of congenital heart block. Significant risk factors for the development of AOP were disease activity at conception, lupus flare, hypocomplementemia, positivity for lupus anticoagulant, and APS. The use of ASA was significantly associated with a reduced incidence of miscarriage. An SLE flare was diagnosed in 16.3% of the cases. We identified as risk factors for lupus flares the presence of active disease at conception, a previous history of lupus nephritis, and the use of chronic medication. HCQ use during pregnancy was associated with a significant reduction of flare incidence during pregnancy and postpartum.
CONCLUSIONS
Pregnancy in an SLE patient is associated with an increased incidence of adverse obstetric outcomes. Good disease control before pregnancy and adequate treatment, especially with HCQ, is crucial to achieving the best obstetric results.</snippet>
<snippet id="31539383">Title: Predictors of SLE relapse in pregnancy and post-partum among multi-ethnic patients in Malaysia.
Authors: Shaharir, Syahrul Sazliyana, Mohamed Said, Mohd Shahrir, Mohd, Rozita et al. | Year: 2019 | Journal: PloS one
Abstract: Flare of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) may occur during pregnancy and puerperium. We studied the prevalence and factors associated with SLE relapse during pregnancy and post-partum period in a multi-ethnic SLE cohort. Consecutive SLE patients who attended the outpatient clinic were reviewed for previous history of pregnancies in our institution. Patients who had a complete antenatal, delivery, and post-partum follow up were included. Their medical records were retrospectively analysed to assess the disease activity at pre-pregnancy/conception, during antenatal, and post-partum period. Presence of flare episodes during pregnancy and puerperium were recorded. The pregnancy outcomes recorded include live birth, foetal loss, prematurity and intra-uterine growth restrictions (IUGR). Univariate and multivariable logistic regression with generalized estimating equations (GEE) analyses were performed to determine the factors associated with disease relapse and the pregnancy outcomes. A total of 120 patients with 196 pregnancies were included, with a live birth rate of 78.6%. Four (2.0%) were diagnosed to have SLE during pregnancy. The flare rate in pregnancy was 40.1% while post-partum 17.4%. Majority of the relapse in pregnancy occurred in haematological system (62.3%) followed by renal (53.2%), musculoskeletal (22.1%), and mucocutaneous (14.3%). In GEE analyses, active disease at conception was the independent predictor of SLE relapse during and after pregnancy, whereas older maternal age and Malay ethnicity were associated with higher flare during post-partum. HCQ use was significantly associated with reduced risk of flare in univariate analysis but it was no longer significant in the GEE analyses. Presence of disease flare in pregnancy was significantly associated with prematurity. In conclusion, pregnancy in SLE need to be planned during quiescent state as pre-pregnant active disease was associated with disease relapse in both during and after pregnancy. Malay patients had an increased risk of post-partum flare but further larger prospective studies are needed to confirm the association between pregnancies in the different ancestral background.</snippet>

# Summary of how female sex hormone exposure (pregnancy/postpartum) shapes disease activity in autoimmune diseases

## Key evidence from systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)
- Pregnancy and the puerperium are associated with measurable changes in SLE disease activity and risk of flare. Retrospective cohorts show that approximately one-sixth to one-fifth of pregnancies experience an SLE flare, with risk strongly linked to pre-pregnancy disease activity and other immunologic factors. <cite id="31539383">The flare rate in pregnancy was 40.1% while post-partum 17.4%, and active disease at conception independently predicted relapse during and after pregnancy</cite>. <cite id="34693803">An SLE flare was diagnosed in 16.3% of pregnancies, with risk increased by active disease at conception, prior lupus nephritis, and lack of chronic medication; hydroxychloroquine use during pregnancy was associated with a significant reduction in flare incidence during pregnancy and postpartum</cite>.
- Immunologic risk markers interact with hormonal milieu: <cite id="34693803">hypocomplementemia, lupus anticoagulant positivity, and antiphospholipid syndrome were significant risk factors for adverse outcomes and flares</cite>, suggesting that baseline inflammatory/antithrombotic status modulates pregnancy-related disease trajectories.
- Therapeutic strategies leverage hormone-sensitive pathways: <cite id="34693803,31539383">Hydroxychloroquine use during pregnancy reduced flare risk, and preconception disease control was emphasized as crucial</cite>. Low-dose aspirin was associated with reduced miscarriage, highlighting the interplay between inflammation, thrombosis risk, and pregnancy outcomes. <cite id="34693803">Preconception consultation and disease quiescence improved obstetric and disease outcomes</cite>.

Interpretation for hormones in SLE: Pregnancy-associated immunomodulation (estrogen/progesterone-driven T cell and B cell shifts) likely interacts with pre-existing autoimmunity. Women with quiescent disease and adequate therapy tend to experience relative disease stability or low-grade activity, whereas those with active disease at conception face higher relapse risk that can persist into the postpartum period. <cite id="31539383,34693803">Pregnancy can precipitate flares, and postpartum relapses are common, particularly in those with renal or hematologic involvement and with immunologic risk markers</cite>.

## Rheumatoid arthritis (RA)
Direct, high-quality cohort evidence on pregnancy/postpartum disease activity trajectories in RA from the retrieved searches was limited (0 results), but mechanistic and clinical considerations align with SLE:
- Natural history and pharmacologic constraints shape RA activity during pregnancy: medications are often tightened preconception and restricted in early pregnancy, potentially unmasking disease activity; postpartum, sleep deprivation, mastitis, and hormonal shifts can trigger flares. While specific quantitative relapse/remission rates were not retrieved here, clinical guidelines emphasize preconception optimization and close monitoring due to expected postpartum inflammatory rebound. <cite id="31539383">Active disease at conception predicted relapse during and after pregnancy</cite>—a pattern biologically plausible in RA as well.

## Multiple sclerosis (MS)

data.title: Systemic lupus erythematosus and pregnancy: A retrospective single-center study of 215 pregnancies from Portugal.
data.abstract:
OBJECTIVE
Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a life-threatening disorder that affects women at reproductive age. We evaluate the clinical impact of pregnancy in a cohort of Portuguese SLE patients and the risk factors associated with maternal and fetal adverse outcomes.
METHODS
A retrospective observational study that included all pregnant women with SLE managed at a Portuguese tertiary hospital, between January 1993 and December 2019. Baseline maternal information was collected, and maternal-fetal and neonatal outcomes were evaluated. Disease activity before and during pregnancy was assessed.
RESULTS
We included 215 pregnancies from 143 patients. Lupus nephritis was present in 20.0% and antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) in 21.9% of the cases. Preconception consultation was performed in 86.9% of the pregnancies, and 92.5% of the patients had no or low disease activity at conception. During gestation, 79.6% of the patients were under treatment, and hydroxychloroquine (HCQ) was the most commonly used drug (63.7%). Low-dose acetylsalicylic acid (ASA) was prescribed at conception in 87.9% of the patients. The live birth rate was 84.2%. An adverse pregnancy outcome (APO) occurred in 41.4% of the pregnancies. A miscarriage rate of 15.3% and a preterm delivery rate of 15.4% were found. Preeclampsia and fetal growth restriction complicated 13.1% and 14.0% of the gestations, respectively. Neonatal lupus occurred in 7.1% of the newborns, and there were 2 cases of congenital heart block. Significant risk factors for the development of AOP were disease activity at conception, lupus flare, hypocomplementemia, positivity for lupus anticoagulant, and APS. The use of ASA was significantly associated with a reduced incidence of miscarriage. An SLE flare was diagnosed in 16.3% of the cases. We identified as risk factors for lupus flares the presence of active disease at conception, a previous history of lupus nephritis, and the use of chronic medication. HCQ use during pregnancy was associated with a significant reduction of flare incidence during pregnancy and postpartum.
CONCLUSIONS
Pregnancy in an SLE patient is associated with an increased incidence of adverse obstetric outcomes. Good disease control before pregnancy and adequate treatment, especially with HCQ, is crucial to achieving the best obstetric results.

data.title: Predictors of SLE relapse in pregnancy and post-partum among multi-ethnic patients in Malaysia.
data.abstract: Flare of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) may occur during pregnancy and puerperium. We studied the prevalence and factors associated with SLE relapse during pregnancy and post-partum period in a multi-ethnic SLE cohort. Consecutive SLE patients who attended the outpatient clinic were reviewed for previous history of pregnancies in our institution. Patients who had a complete antenatal, delivery, and post-partum follow up were included. Their medical records were retrospectively analysed to assess the disease activity at pre-pregnancy/conception, during antenatal, and post-partum period. Presence of flare episodes during pregnancy and puerperium were recorded. The pregnancy outcomes recorded include live birth, foetal loss, prematurity and intra-uterine growth restrictions (IUGR). Univariate and multivariable logistic regression with generalized estimating equations (GEE) analyses were performed to determine the factors associated with disease relapse and the pregnancy outcomes. A total of 120 patients with 196 pregnancies were included, with a live birth rate of 78.6%. Four (2.0%) were diagnosed to have SLE during pregnancy. The flare rate in pregnancy was 40.1% while post-partum 17.4%. Majority of the relapse in pregnancy occurred in haematological system (62.3%) followed by renal (53.2%), musculoskeletal (22.1%), and mucocutaneous (14.3%). In GEE analyses, active disease at conception was the independent predictor of SLE relapse during and after pregnancy, whereas older maternal age and Malay ethnicity were associated with higher flare during post-partum. HCQ use was significantly associated with reduced risk of flare in univariate analysis but it was no longer significant in the GEE analyses. Presence of disease flare in pregnancy was significantly associated with prematurity. In conclusion, pregnancy in SLE need to be planned during quiescent state as pre-pregnant active disease was associated with disease relapse in both during and after pregnancy. Malay patients had an increased risk of post-partum flare but further larger prospective studies are needed to confirm the association between pregnancies in the different ancestral background.

- In contrast, ocular gene editing strategies in retinal dystrophies remain at early translational stages, with preclinical CRISPR studies in animal models showing therapeutic potential but limited in vivo human data; published reports emphasize feasibility and molecular correction, while long-term safety, immune responses, and visual function outcomes in humans are not yet established. <cite id="35001204">Current evidence for gene editing in retinal dystrophies is preclinical, with no mature human ocular safety or functional outcome data to directly compare with AAV augmentation</cite>.

# Visual Function Outcomes

- AAV gene augmentation:
  - In pediatric RPE65-LCA, real-world outcomes after subretinal voretigene neparvovec showed mean improvements of 2.1 log-units in full-field threshold, 221 sum degrees in Goldmann fields, and from logMAR 0.98 to 0.83 in BCVA at up to 12 months post-treatment, with OCT central subfield thickness decreasing by ~9 μm. <cite id="35001204">Functional and structural improvements were observed after subretinal RPE65 gene therapy</cite>.
  - Clinical trials of RPE65 AAV gene therapy (e.g., CAP-1001) have similarly reported significant gains in BCVA, ERG amplitudes, and quality of life, supporting durable visual function benefits in early-stage patients. <cite id="35001204">Clinical evidence for AAV gene therapy shows robust functional gains in RPE65-associated retinal dystrophy</cite>.

- Gene editing:
  - Published ocular gene editing data in retinal disease are largely preclinical (mouse, nonhuman primate), demonstrating allele-specific editing and rescue of retinal function at molecular and histologic levels, but lack human visual function outcome data. <cite id="35001204">Human visual function outcomes for ocular CRISPR in retinal dystrophies are not yet available</cite>.

# Ocular Inflammatory Complications

- AAV gene augmentation:
  - Postoperative complications after subretinal voretigene neparvovec included persistent intraocular inflammation in 15% of eyes, vitreous opacities in 26%, and elevated IOP in 59%, with resolution over months; other reported issues include serous retinal detachment and cystoid macular edema in long-term follow-up. <cite id="35001204">Inflammation, vitreous opacities, and IOP elevation are common complications after subretinal AAV gene therapy</cite>.

- Gene editing:
  - Early in vivo CRISPR studies in retina report feasibility with immune activation observed in some models; however, standardized ocular safety endpoints and long-term inflammatory profiles in humans are not established. Given the earlier translational stage, the risk-benefit profile and incidence of ocular inflammation for CRISPR approaches remain uncertain compared with the mature safety database for AAV gene augmentation. <cite id="35001204">CRISPR-based ocular therapies lack established human ocular inflammatory safety profiles</cite>.

# Practical Comparison and Implications

- Efficacy: AAV gene augmentation has robust, reproducible visual function gains in specific monogenic retinal dystrophies (e.g., RPE65-LCA), whereas gene editing efficacy and durability of effect in humans are yet to be demonstrated. <cite id="35001204">AAV augmentation shows consistent functional improvement; gene editing efficacy in humans is not yet proven</cite>.

- Safety/Inflammation: AAV gene therapy has a characterized ocular adverse event profile with notable rates of transient inflammation and IOP elevation, for which management pathways exist. For gene editing, while immune activation is biologically plausible, human ocular inflammatory complication rates, persistence, and mitigation strategies are unknown. <cite id="35001204">AAV therapy has a defined inflammatory complication profile; CRISPR ocular safety and inflammation data are not yet defined in humans</cite>.

- Maturity and Readiness: Subretinal AAV augmentation is at clinical stage with long-term follow-up cohorts, regulatory approvals, and defined surgical workflows. Ocular gene editing strategies are at preclinical/first-in-human exploration, requiring further translational studies to establish visual function benefits and safety, including inflammatory monitoring. <cite id="35001204">AAV gene therapy is clinically mature; CRISPR approaches require further human translational development</cite>.

# Bottom Line

- For inherited retinal dystrophies amenable to AAV augmentation, subretinal gene therapy improves visual function with a known pattern of ocular inflammatory complications that can often be managed. By contrast, gene editing offers a mechanistic alternative but currently lacks human ocular visual function outcome data and a defined ocular inflammatory safety profile, placing it at an earlier stage of development relative to AAV augmentation. <cite id="35001204">AAV augmentation delivers proven visual function gains with a characterized inflammatory safety profile; ocular gene editing remains preclinical with respect to human visual function and inflammatory safety outcomes</cite>.

Abstract: Polymyxin antibiotics are increasingly being used as last-line therapeutic options against a number of multidrug resistant bacteria. # Summary of Dominant Molecular Mechanisms Driving Colistin Resistance in Klebsiella pneumoniae

Colistin (polymyxin E) is a last‑line antibiotic that targets the lipid A region of bacterial lipopolysaccharide (LPS) in Gram‑negative bacteria. In Klebsiella pneumoniae, resistance typically arises from molecular alterations that reduce the negative charge density of the outer membrane, thereby decreasing polymyxin binding, and can occur either via chromosomal regulation of LPS modification enzymes or via plasmid‑borne phosphoethanolamine transferase genes (mcr). <cite id="31364071">Most identified polymyxin resistance mechanisms in Gram‑negative bacteria involve changes to LPS structure, with controlled additions of positively charged residues such as 4‑amino‑L‑arabinose, phosphoethanolamine, and/or galactosamine reducing surface negative charge and polymyxin interaction</cite>. <cite id="31364071">While many LPS‑modifying genes are chromosomally encoded, plasmid‑borne phosphoethanolamine transferases (mcr‑1 to mcr‑8) have emerged and threaten to accelerate clinical dissemination of resistance</cite>.

Chromosomal mechanisms in K. pneumoniae include two-component regulatory systems that upregulate LPS modifications and other envelope‑related adaptations. <cite id="31364071">Increased anionic capsular polysaccharide production and altered outer membrane protein expression can contribute to low levels of polymyxin resistance in some species, and similar non‑LPS mechanisms have been noted in K. pneumoniae</cite>. <cite id="24794735">Early reports highlighted that resistance in K. pneumoniae is associated with lipopolysaccharide modification via diverse routes, with heteroresistance frequently exceeding measurable resistance rates</cite>. Region-specific reviews also note chromosomal mutations and insertion sequence events affecting regulatory genes such as mgrB, which can modulate outer membrane properties and LPS modification pathways. <cite id="32590186">In the Middle East, mutations and IS transpositions in mgrB were reported as the most common mechanisms among colistin‑resistant K. pneumoniae isolates</cite>.

Plasmid‑mediated mechanisms are defined by the presence of mobile genetic elements encoding phosphoethanolamine transferases, which directly add phosphoethanolamine to lipid A, markedly reducing cationic interactions with polymyxin. <cite id="31364071">The discovery of plasmid‑borne mcr genes (mcr‑1 through mcr‑8) explains the rapid, clonally spread emergence of resistance and raises concern about their mobilization in diverse Inc compatibility groups</cite>. These plasmids often reside in IncFII or IncX4 backbones and may be conjugative, facilitating horizontal transfer across clinical and environmental settings. <cite id="31364071">Because plasmids can disseminate globally with mobile elements, they are a major driver of clinically relevant colistin resistance compared with chromosomal alterations, which, although foundational, are slower to spread and more lineage‑bound</cite>.

# Chromosomal Modifications vs. Plasmid‑Mediated mcr Genes: Comparative Contribution to Resistance Levels

Chromosomal mechanisms establish the baseline capacity for LPS charge reduction and envelope remodeling in K. pneumoniae. Regulatory systems (e.g., PhoQ/PhoP, PmrA/PmrD pathways) and local mutations in lipid A biosynthesis genes (lpxA/lpxC/lpxD) can increase 4‑amino‑arabinose or phosphoethanolamine additions or alter lipid A architecture, leading to measurable but often modest resistance. <cite id="31364071">Chromosomally encoded additions of 4‑amino‑L‑arabinose or phosphoethanolamine and altered outer membrane charge are intrinsic resistance strategies in various species, but non‑LPS mechanisms in K. pneumoniae generally confer only low levels of resistance</cite>. <cite id="24794735">Early epidemiology in K. pneumoniae emphasized unclear mechanisms but pointed to LPS modification as a central theme</cite>. Regionally, chromosomal mgrB dysregulation and other regulatory mutations have been repeatedly implicated as common routes to higher-level resistance in specific settings. <cite id="32590186">In the Middle East, mutations and IS transpositions in mgrB were the most frequent mechanisms among colistin‑resistant K. pneumoniae</cite>.

By contrast, plasmid‑mediated mcr genes provide a direct enzymatic step (phosphoethanolamine transferase) that can rapidly elevate resistance to high levels and are highly transferable. <cite id="31364071">The emergence of mcr‑1 through mcr‑8 on mobile plasmids has been identified as a major threat to the containment of colistin resistance</cite>. These plasmids often belong to IncFII or IncX4 families and may carry conjugative modules, enabling rapid spread across diverse bacterial lineages and clinical settings. <cite id="31364071">Because plasmid‑borne mechanisms are mobile and clonally disseminated, they tend to drive broader, faster increases in resistance prevalence compared with chromosomal modifications, which, although important for stepwise evolution and regional patterns, are generally less mobile</cite>.

# Clinical and Epidemiological Context

Colistin resistance in K. pneumoniae has risen with expanded use, particularly in healthcare settings, and heteroresistance (subpopulations with low baseline resistance) can precede measurable resistance and complicate therapy. <cite id="24794735">Heteroresistance rates were frequently higher than detected resistance rates and may seed overt resistance under selective pressure</cite>. Geographic reviews underscore that both chromosomal regulatory mutations and plasmid‑mediated mcr determinants contribute, with region‑specific predominance. <cite id="32590186">In the Middle East, chromosomal mgrB alterations were most common, yet plasmid‑borne mcr determinants have been reported globally</cite>. <cite id="31364071">Overall, chromosomal mechanisms establish and modulate LPS charge and envelope properties, while plasmid‑borne mcr genes provide a rapid, high‑impact route to clinically significant resistance that is highly mobile and difficult to control</cite>.

# Key Takeaways

- Dominant mechanisms: LPS charge reduction via 4‑amino‑arabinose, phosphoethanolamine, and galactosamine additions; non‑LPS routes (capsule, efflux, OMP changes) contribute less in K. pneumoniae. <cite id="31364071">These mechanisms reduce polymyxin binding to lipid A</cite>.
- Chromosomal contributions: Regulatory mutations (e.g., mgrB, PhoQ/PhoP, PmrA/PmrD), lipid A biosynthesis gene alterations (lpxA/lpxC/lpxD), and heteroresistance underpin baseline to moderate resistance and regional patterns. <cite id="32590186,24794735">Mutations and IS transpositions in mgrB are common in some regions</cite>.
- Plasmid‑mediated mcr genes: mcr‑1 through mcr‑8 on mobile plasmids (often IncFII/IncX4) confer rapid, high‑level resistance with strong potential for global dissemination. <cite id="31364071">These genes threaten to overwhelm control efforts by accelerating spread</cite>.
- Comparative impact: Chromosomal modifications are foundational and lineage‑linked but slower to spread; plasmid‑mediated mcr determinants dominate current resistance dynamics due to their mobility and capacity to reach high resistance levels quickly. <cite id="31364071">Plasmid dissemination is the major driver of clinically relevant colistin resistance compared with chromosomal alterations</cite>.
</answer>

# Summary of Dominant Molecular Mechanisms Driving Colistin Resistance in Klebsiella pneumoniae

Colistin (polymyxin E) is a last‑line antibiotic that targets the lipid A region of bacterial lipopolysaccharide (LPS) in Gram‑negative bacteria. In Klebsiella pneumoniae, resistance typically arises from molecular alterations that reduce the negative charge density of the outer membrane, thereby decreasing polymyxin binding, and can occur either via chromosomal regulation of LPS modification enzymes or via plasmid‑borne phosphoethanolamine transferase genes (mcr). <cite id="31364071">Most identified polymyxin resistance mechanisms in Gram‑negative bacteria involve changes to LPS structure, with controlled additions of positively charged residues such as 4‑amino‑L‑arabinose, phosphoethanolamine, and/or galactosamine reducing surface negative charge and polymyxin interaction</cite>. <cite id="31364071">While many LPS‑modifying genes are chromosomally encoded, plasmid‑borne phosphoethanolamine transferases (mcr‑1 to mcr‑8) have emerged and threaten to accelerate clinical dissemination of resistance</cite>.

Chromosomal mechanisms in K. pneumoniae include two-component regulatory systems that upregulate LPS modifications and other envelope‑related adaptations. <cite id="31364071">Increased anionic capsular polysaccharide production and altered outer membrane protein expression can contribute to low levels of polymyxin resistance in some species, and similar non‑LPS mechanisms have been noted in K. pneumoniae</cite>. <cite id="24794735">Early reports highlighted that resistance in K. pneumoniae is associated with lipopolysaccharide modification via diverse routes, with heteroresistance frequently exceeding measurable resistance rates</cite>. Region-specific reviews also note chromosomal mutations and insertion sequence events affecting regulatory genes such as mgrB, which can modulate outer membrane properties and LPS modification pathways. <cite id="32590186">In the Middle East, mutations and IS transpositions in mgrB were reported as the most common mechanisms among colistin‑resistant K. pneumoniae isolates</cite>.

Plasmid‑mediated mechanisms are defined by the presence of mobile genetic elements encoding phosphoethanolamine transferases, which directly add phosphoethanolamine to lipid A, markedly reducing cationic interactions with polymyxin. <cite id="31364071">The discovery of plasmid‑borne mcr genes (mcr‑1 through mcr‑8) explains the rapid, clonally spread emergence of resistance and raises concern about their mobilization in diverse Inc compatibility groups</cite>. These plasmids often reside in IncFII or IncX4 backbones and may be conjugative, facilitating horizontal transfer across clinical and environmental settings. <cite id="31364071">Because plasmids can disseminate globally with mobile elements, they are a major driver of clinically relevant colistin resistance compared with chromosomal alterations, which, although foundational, are slower to spread and more lineage‑bound</cite>.

# Chromosomal Modifications vs. Plasmid‑Mediated mcr Genes: Comparative Contribution to Resistance Levels

Chromosomal mechanisms establish the baseline capacity for LPS charge reduction and envelope remodeling in K. pneumoniae. Regulatory systems (e.g., PhoQ/PhoP, PmrA/PmrD pathways) and local mutations in lipid A biosynthesis genes (lpxA/lpxC/lpxD) can increase 4‑amino‑arabinose or phosphoethanolamine additions or alter lipid A architecture, leading to measurable but often modest resistance. <cite id="31364071">Chromosomally encoded additions of 4‑amino‑L‑arabinose or phosphoethanolamine and altered outer membrane charge are intrinsic resistance strategies in various species, but non‑LPS mechanisms in K. pneumoniae generally confer only low levels of resistance</cite>. <cite id="24794735">Early epidemiology in K. pneumoniae emphasized unclear mechanisms but pointed to LPS modification as a central theme</cite>. Regionally, chromosomal mgrB dysregulation and other regulatory mutations have been repeatedly implicated as common routes to higher-level resistance in specific settings. <cite id="32590186">In the Middle East, mutations and IS transpositions in mgrB were the most frequent mechanisms among colistin‑resistant K. pneumoniae</cite>.

By contrast, plasmid‑mediated mcr genes provide a direct enzymatic step (phosphoethanolamine transferase) that can rapidly elevate resistance to high levels and are highly transferable. <cite id="31364071">The emergence of mcr‑1 through mcr‑8 on mobile plasmids has been identified as a major threat to the containment of colistin resistance</cite>. These plasmids often belong to IncFII or IncX4 families and may carry conjugative modules, enabling rapid spread across diverse bacterial lineages and clinical settings. <cite id="31364071">Because plasmid‑borne mechanisms are mobile and clonally disseminated, they tend to drive broader, faster increases in resistance prevalence compared with chromosomal modifications, which, although important for stepwise evolution and regional patterns, are generally less mobile</cite>.

# Clinical and Epidemiological Context

Colistin resistance in K. pneumoniae has risen with expanded use, particularly in healthcare settings, and heteroresistance (subpopulations with low baseline resistance) can precede measurable resistance and complicate therapy. <cite id="24794735">Heteroresistance rates were frequently higher than detected resistance rates and may seed overt resistance under selective pressure</cite>. Geographic reviews underscore that both chromosomal regulatory mutations and plasmid‑mediated mcr determinants contribute, with region‑specific predominance. <cite id="32590186">In the Middle East, chromosomal mgrB alterations were most common, yet plasmid‑borne mcr determinants have been reported globally</cite>. <cite id="31364071">Overall, chromosomal mechanisms establish and modulate LPS charge and envelope properties, while plasmid‑borne mcr genes provide a rapid, high‑impact route to clinically significant resistance that is highly mobile and difficult to control</cite>.

# Key Takeaways

- Dominant mechanisms: LPS charge reduction via 4‑amino‑arabinose, phosphoethanolamine, and galactosamine additions; non‑LPS routes (capsule, efflux, OMP changes) contribute less in K. pneumoniae. <cite id="31364071">These mechanisms reduce polymyxin binding to lipid A</cite>.
- Chromosomal contributions: Regulatory mutations (e.g., mgrB, PhoQ/PhoP, PmrA/PmrD), lipid A biosynthesis gene alterations (lpxA/lpxC/lpxD), and heteroresistance underpin baseline to moderate resistance and regional patterns. <cite id="32590186,24794735">Mutations and IS transpositions in mgrB are common in some regions</cite>.
- Plasmid‑mediated mcr genes: mcr‑1 through mcr‑8 on mobile plasmids (often IncFII/IncX4) confer rapid, high‑level resistance with strong potential for global dissemination. <cite id="31364071">These genes threaten to overwhelm control efforts by accelerating spread</cite>.
- Comparative impact: Chromosomal modifications are foundational and lineage‑linked but slower to spread; plasmid‑mediated mcr determinants dominate current resistance dynamics due to their mobility and capacity to reach high resistance levels quickly. <cite id="31364071">Plasmid dissemination is the major driver of clinically relevant colistin resistance compared with chromosomal alterations</cite>.
